execrable

/EK-sih-kruh-buhl/ - the stress falls on EK · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Execrable means loathsome; dreadfully bad.

The critic spared the airport hotel exactly one word on the comment card — execrable — and underlined it twice.

Example

The apartment's previous tenant had repainted every room himself, and the landlord walked the new couple through the results in apologetic silence: drips fossilized down the switch plates, a ceiling half rolled in a second shade of white, tape lines drifting through every corner. 'execrable' was the word the building inspector wrote, and nobody argued.

Execrable sits at the bottom of the scale of bad: not disappointing, not shoddy, but work so wretched it feels like an offense to whoever must look at it. The word began as a literal curse — 'deserving to be cursed' — and it keeps that heat; save it for the failures that make people swear.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

abominable: Abominable condemns on moral grounds as much as on quality — we call cruelty, betrayals, and inhuman conditions abominable. Execrable stays a judgment of quality: work, performances, food so wretchedly bad they feel like an insult. An abominable act outrages the conscience; an execrable film only ruins the evening.

atrocious: Atrocious is the everyday exaggeration for anything shockingly bad — atrocious traffic, atrocious handwriting — reached for casually and forgotten by dinner. Execrable is rarer and hotter, a formal curse a reviewer chooses deliberately, and it lands with the weight of a verdict rather than a groan.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

superb: of the highest quality

admirable: deserving open praise

Where it sits · how deep the badness runs

shoddy → dreadful → execrable

shoddy vs. execrable: Shoddy work cuts corners and shows it; execrable lives several floors further down.

dreadful vs. execrable: Dreadful is very bad indeed, but execrable is the final rung — badness that invites cursing, the review written in a hiss.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — execr: to curse (Latin exsecrari: ex- 'out of' + sacrare 'to declare sacred')

Suffix — -able: deserving to be

Put it together: Execr (to curse) + -able (here 'deserving to be') = deserving to be cursed. Latin exsecrari was built from ex- ('out of') and sacrare ('to declare sacred'): to execrate something was to cast it out of the sacred and call curses down on it. English keeps the verb — critics still execrate what they cannot forgive — and the adjective keeps the temperature: not merely bad, but curse-worthy. Note the suffix's second job here: -able usually means 'able to be,' but in words like lovable and execrable it means 'worthy to be.'

Use the root in a new word: sacred: The grove was sacred to the villagers, and no axe was ever carried past its first ring of stones.

Strength Check

Word Choice

literary / scathing

Execrable is a curse in evening dress — reviewers' language for quality so low it offends. For garden-variety failure, poor or shoddy will do; save execrable for the performance that makes you want your hour back, and expect it to raise eyebrows at the dinner table.
